concepts.definition: Replace particular object identities with variables or roles while retaining relevant types and relations.

citations.section: Variabilization

concepts.definition: A non-instance that can expose a missing restriction; a closely contrasting negative is often called a near miss.

citations.section: Negative example

concepts.definition: Require a necessary relation or exclude a disqualifying relation.

citations.section: Require-link / forbid-link

concepts.definition: Generalization heuristics that change relations, allowed values, category level, or numeric bounds.

citations.section: Drop-link / enlarge-set / climb-tree / close-interval

concepts.definition: Establish a plausible broader category, then test more specific candidates using discriminating knowledge.

citations.section: Establish-and-refine

concepts.definition: A concept characterized by necessary and sufficient membership conditions in its stated domain.

citations.section: Axiomatic concept

concepts.definition: Represent a class through typical features or remembered instances respectively.

citations.section: Prototype concept / exemplar concept

concepts.definition: The stated knowledge and the procedure that draws conclusions from it.

citations.section: Knowledge base / inference engine

concepts.definition: Only entailed conclusions are derived / every entailed conclusion is derivable in the specified setting.

citations.section: Soundness / completeness

concepts.definition: Infer q from p and p -> q / infer NOT p from NOT q and p -> q.

citations.section: Modus ponens / modus tollens

concepts.definition: Prove a query by adding its negation to clause-form premises and resolving complementary literals to derive a contradiction.

citations.section: Resolution theorem proving

concepts.definition: A conjunction of clauses, with each clause a disjunction of literals; a literal is an atom or its negation.

citations.section: Conjunctive normal form

concepts.definition: For every value / for at least one value in the stated domain.

citations.section: Universal / existential quantifier

concepts.definition: A condition needed before an operator can be applied.

citations.section: Precondition

concepts.definition: What holds after the operator; often described using added and deleted facts, or effects.

citations.section: Postcondition

concepts.definition: Order only the steps that need an ordering to preserve a valid plan.

citations.section: Partial order

concepts.definition: Refine an abstract task into lower-level tasks.

citations.section: Hierarchical decomposition

concepts.definition: How an entity participates in an event, such as agent, object, or instrument.

citations.section: Thematic role

concepts.definition: A restriction that rules out unsuitable role fillers or interpretations.

citations.section: Constraint

concepts.definition: More than one possible interpretation that may need context to resolve.

citations.section: Ambiguity

concepts.definition: A primitive action describing a change in physical location of an object, including an agent moving itself.

citations.section: Move-object

concepts.definition: A primitive action describing a transfer of possession, which need not be identical to physical movement.

citations.section: Move-possession

concepts.definition: Examples of other primitive actions in the ebook; choose using meaning and context.

citations.section: Ingest / propel / speak

concepts.definition: An action inferred from the representation and context rather than stated directly.

citations.section: Implied action

concepts.definition: A structured pattern for a recurring sequence of events.

citations.section: Script

concepts.definition: What makes a script applicable / what is expected after its events.

citations.section: Entry conditions / results

concepts.definition: Participants / objects / stages in the event sequence.

citations.section: Roles / props / scenes

concepts.definition: A context-dependent variation of a script.

citations.section: Track

concepts.definition: The domain knowledge used to explain why the example works.

citations.section: Prior knowledge

concepts.definition: Keep the explanation-relevant structure while leaving out incidental details.

citations.section: Abstraction

concepts.definition: Use that useful structure in another situation.

citations.section: Transfer

concepts.definition: Similarity of appearance / relationships / purpose.

citations.section: Superficial / structural / pragmatic similarity

concepts.definition: Align corresponding objects and relations in source and target.

citations.section: Analogical mapping

concepts.definition: Project candidate knowledge from the source into the target.

citations.section: Analogical transfer

concepts.definition: All hypotheses in the chosen language consistent with the examples.

citations.section: Version space

concepts.definition: The specific side of the source’s version-space account; positive examples call for generalization of the specific model.

citations.section: Specific model

concepts.definition: The general side of the source’s version-space account; negative examples call for specialization of the general model.

citations.section: General model

concepts.definition: Use restrictions to narrow possibilities and pass the consequences to related variables.

citations.section: Constraint propagation

concepts.definition: Assign interpretations to edges subject to junction and neighboring-edge constraints.

citations.section: Line labeling

concepts.definition: Restrictions on combinations of values. Local support is not a general proof that all constraints can be satisfied together.

citations.section: Constraints

concepts.definition: Select and arrange known components under constraints.

citations.section: Configuration

concepts.definition: Design using a known repertoire of components.

citations.section: Routine design

concepts.definition: The result sought / a way to achieve it.

citations.section: Task / method

concepts.definition: Observed information / candidate fault explanations.

citations.section: Data space / hypothesis space

concepts.definition: Propose a cause that could explain an observed effect.

citations.section: Abduction

concepts.definition: How much of the observed evidence the explanation accounts for.

citations.section: Explanatory coverage

concepts.definition: A preference for a smaller or simpler explanation, other things being equal.

citations.section: Parsimony

concepts.definition: Notice a difference between expected and observed behavior.

citations.section: Error detection

concepts.definition: Locate the knowledge or decision responsible for the failure.

citations.section: Blame assignment

concepts.definition: Change the responsible knowledge or reasoning and test the consequence.

citations.section: Repair

concepts.definition: A goal to acquire knowledge needed to repair a detected gap, for example connecting two parts of an incomplete explanation.

citations.section: Learning goal

concepts.definition: Choose a method / combine methods.

citations.section: Strategy selection / integration

concepts.definition: Generate or revise goals in response to expectations, failures, or knowledge gaps.

citations.section: Goal-based autonomy

concepts.definition: Reasoning over a representation that preserves spatial structure.

citations.section: Visuospatial reasoning

concepts.definition: Connecting a symbol's meaning with perception and the world.

citations.section: Symbol grounding

concepts.definition: Components and relations / causal processes / intended purpose.

citations.section: Structure-Behavior-Function

concepts.definition: Newness / a non-obvious or surprising outcome, discussed as aspects of creativity.

citations.section: Novelty / unexpectedness

concepts.definition: What knowledge is expressed / how it is used.

citations.section: Representation / reasoning

concepts.definition: How knowledge changes / how it is stored and retrieved.

citations.section: Learning / memory

concepts.definition: Reasoning about the agent’s own reasoning, learning, or reactive processes; monitoring a strategy and changing it is different from solving the external task.

citations.section: Metacognition

concepts.definition: A language and its expressed knowledge content, structured so a reasoning method can use relevant objects, properties, and relations.

citations.section: Knowledge representation

concepts.definition: Using available knowledge to infer, decide, interpret, or solve a problem; it interacts with learning and memory rather than operating in isolation.

citations.section: Reasoning

concepts.definition: A system whose interacting components aim at human-like intelligence and are situated in a physical and potentially social environment.

citations.section: Cognitive system

concepts.definition: Building and evaluating computational models on intelligence-test tasks, using performance and mechanisms to investigate cognition rather than equating test success with general intelligence.

citations.section: Computational psychometrics

concepts.definition: The historical visual-analogy test used to discuss computational psychometrics in the 2016 ebook; it is not the Fall2026 ARC-AGI assignment specification.

citations.section: Raven’s Progressive Matrices

concepts.definition: Reusing a regularity beyond the particular observations from which it was obtained; successful reuse depends on which structure is preserved.

citations.section: Generalizing knowledge

concepts.definition: The vocabulary of symbols available in a representation, such as object nodes and relation labels.

citations.section: Lexicon

concepts.definition: The rules for composing representation symbols, including the direction and connectivity of links.

citations.section: Structure

concepts.definition: The interpretation of a representation that makes some inferences legitimate; merely drawing an edge does not establish its meaning.

citations.section: Semantics

concepts.definition: The component that proposes candidates; knowledge can restrict generation to relevant, legal, or nonredundant possibilities.

citations.section: Generator

concepts.definition: The component that checks a proposed candidate; legality, duplication, and goal satisfaction are distinct possible tests.

citations.section: Tester

concepts.definition: A generator that incorporates useful knowledge before materializing candidates, while preserving alternatives needed by the task.

citations.section: Smart generator

concepts.definition: The represented states and possible transitions obtained by applying operators, with the chosen abstraction determining what counts as a state.

citations.section: State space

concepts.definition: A task-relevant mismatch between current and desired state, used to guide choice; it need not equal true remaining solution cost.

citations.section: Difference

concepts.definition: A represented action that changes a state when its applicability conditions hold.

citations.section: Operator

concepts.definition: Rapidly changing current facts and goals used to activate productions; it is distinct from the more persistent rule store.

citations.section: Working memory

concepts.definition: Procedural knowledge expressed as a condition and a consequence or action, matched against current working memory.

citations.section: Production rule

concepts.definition: Learning a production that captures knowledge useful for resolving an impasse, so a similar future choice can be made without repeating the full resolution.

citations.section: Chunking

concepts.definition: A named attribute or relation in a frame; it specifies a role for a value rather than being that value.

citations.section: Slot

concepts.definition: The value occupying a slot, potentially a reference to another frame rather than an isolated scalar.

citations.section: Filler

concepts.definition: An expected filler used in the absence of more specific information; it can be overridden and must not be treated as an exceptionless fact.

citations.section: Default value

concepts.definition: An encapsulated past experience represented with information useful for comparing a new problem and reusing an earlier solution.

citations.section: Case

concepts.definition: The stored case minimizing a declared distance to the query representation; proximity is a retrieval claim, not a guarantee of solution suitability.

citations.section: Nearest neighbor

concepts.definition: The comparison rule that determines which differences matter in retrieval; feature choice and scaling shape the result.

citations.section: Similarity metric

concepts.definition: Use the current problem as a probe to find relevant prior experience; relevance depends on how cases were represented and indexed.

citations.section: Case retrieval

concepts.definition: Change a retrieved solution to address differences between its original problem and the current problem.

citations.section: Case adaptation

concepts.definition: Assess a proposed adapted solution against the new requirements, using suitable simulation, execution, or critique.

citations.section: Case evaluation

concepts.definition: Retain an evaluated problem–solution experience with useful context so it can support future retrieval.

citations.section: Case storage

concepts.definition: Revise a concept description one labelled example at a time; generalize for an uncovered positive and specialize for a covered negative.

citations.section: Incremental concept learning

concepts.definition: A negative example closely resembling a positive or current description, useful because a focused difference can reveal a required or forbidden relation.

citations.section: Near miss

concepts.definition: Generalize by removing a relation from the concept description when a positive example shows that the relation is not required.

citations.section: Drop-link

concepts.definition: Specialize by making a relation mandatory when a negative example missing it would otherwise be covered.

citations.section: Require-link

concepts.definition: Specialize by prohibiting a relation present in a covered negative example.

citations.section: Forbid-link

concepts.definition: Generalize a discrete allowed-value set by adding a new accepted alternative.

citations.section: Enlarge-set

concepts.definition: Generalize using background taxonomy knowledge to replace particular alternatives with an appropriate shared superclass.

citations.section: Climb-tree

concepts.definition: Revise a numerical range to include a positive value outside the previous range; the source illustrates enlarging the accepted size interval.

citations.section: Close-interval

concepts.definition: Prior relational or taxonomic knowledge that constrains what to generalize and permits abstraction beyond observed alternatives.

citations.section: Background knowledge

concepts.definition: Assign an instance to a concept or category under a stated membership representation and procedure.

citations.section: Classification

concepts.definition: A grouping that treats items as equivalent with respect to a selected classification criterion, not identical in every property.

citations.section: Equivalence class

concepts.definition: An organization of more general and more specific concepts, whose links must preserve the intended category relation.

citations.section: Concept hierarchy

concepts.definition: A concept represented through typical properties that can be overridden for particular members.

citations.section: Prototype concept

concepts.definition: A concept represented through examples where an agreed set of necessary or even typical conditions may be difficult to state.

citations.section: Exemplar concept

concepts.definition: Reason from an instance’s observed features toward compatible concepts rather than starting only with a broad candidate and refining downward.

citations.section: Bottom-up search

concepts.definition: The explicitly stated sentences an agent uses as premises; logical inference preserves their consequences but does not establish their real-world truth.

citations.section: Knowledge base

concepts.definition: The procedure applying licensed inference rules to a knowledge base; representation and proof search must be distinguished.

citations.section: Inference engine

concepts.definition: An expression assigning truth to a property or relation of its arguments under an interpretation.

citations.section: Predicate

concepts.definition: A sentence is entailed when it is true in every interpretation satisfying the knowledge base.

citations.section: Entailment

concepts.definition: The property that derived conclusions are entailed by the premises in the stated logical setting, not a guarantee that the premises describe reality accurately.

citations.section: Soundness

concepts.definition: The property that every entailed conclusion is derivable by the proof system in the stated setting; it does not make search cheap.

citations.section: Completeness

concepts.definition: From P and P implies Q, infer Q.

citations.section: Modus ponens

concepts.definition: From not Q and P implies Q, infer not P.

citations.section: Modus tollens

concepts.definition: A quantifier stating that a condition applies for every value of a variable in the declared domain.

citations.section: Universal quantifier

concepts.definition: A quantifier stating that at least one value in the declared domain satisfies the quantified condition.

citations.section: Existential quantifier

concepts.definition: The interacting processes of reasoning, learning, and memory that use knowledge to choose what to do, rather than mapping a percept directly to an action.

citations.section: Deliberation

concepts.definition: A direct percept-to-action mapping that need not construct a plan. It is an architectural role, not a claim that the behavior is unintelligent.

citations.section: Reaction

concepts.definition: Changing available knowledge through experience or instruction, with what and when to learn constrained by the agent’s reasoning needs.

citations.section: Learning

concepts.definition: Storing learned knowledge and making relevant knowledge available to reasoning; retrieval is as important as accumulation.

citations.section: Memory

concepts.definition: The perspectives formed by thinking versus acting and human-like versus rational evaluation. A system can support more than one perspective.

citations.section: Four schools of AI

concepts.definition: Express a task and relevant knowledge in a representation, then apply a reasoning method whose operations use that representation.

citations.section: Represent and reason

concepts.definition: Using hypotheses about human cognition to inform AI designs, and AI mechanisms to generate testable hypotheses about human cognition.

citations.section: Cognitive connection

chapters.title: Introduction to Knowledge-Based AI
chapters.summary: Knowledge-based AI studies how represented knowledge supports reasoning, learning, and memory in agents with limited resources.

citations.section: Conundrums in AI; Characteristics of AI Problems; Characteristics of AI Agents

blocks.title: Why knowledge matters under limits
blocks.text:
The course begins with a tension: intelligent agents have limited computation, sensors, attention, and knowledge, but face large, changing, open-ended problems. Information arrives incrementally and similar situations recur. An agent cannot simply enumerate everything or wait until it knows the whole world before acting.

The five conundrums make that tension concrete: limited resources versus difficult computation; local operations versus global constraints; deductive computation versus inductive or abductive tasks; existing knowledge versus new situations; and solving a problem versus also explaining the solution. Knowledge-based AI investigates how useful abstractions, remembered experience, and reasoning methods can address these limits. Bounded rationality means reasoning under such bounds, not possession of a universally optimal answer.

citations.section: Exercise AI in Practice Watson; What is Knowledge-Based AI

blocks.title: Reasoning, learning, and memory work together
blocks.text:
Watson answering a Jeopardy clue makes the components visible: it must interpret the clue, access relevant knowledge, choose an answer, and express it appropriately. The lesson groups interpretation and decision making under reasoning. Learning changes what the agent knows; memory stores that knowledge and makes it available when needed.

These are mutually dependent processes. Reasoning draws on memory and can produce information worth retaining. Learning needs existing knowledge and supplies future reasoning. The course calls this interacting group deliberation. Studying only an answer-producing algorithm would miss how the knowledge it uses was acquired, organized, and retrieved.

blocks.title: Human-like and rational are different aims
blocks.text:
The four schools cross two distinctions: thinking versus acting, and human-like versus rational or optimal performance. Thinking concerns internal reasoning; acting concerns behavior in the world. A human-like account aims to capture aspects of human cognition or behavior; a rational account asks whether inference or action meets an appropriate standard for the task.

The autonomous-car discussion shows why these distinctions matter: reaching a destination safely does not require reproducing a particular person’s driving habits. Conversely, studying human problem solving can inform an artificial agent even when the agent is evaluated on task success. The categories are perspectives, not exclusive labels for every feature of a complex system. KBAI’s cognitive-systems emphasis keeps the connection to human cognition central.

citations.section: What are Cognitive Systems; Cognitive System Architecture

blocks.title: Reaction, deliberation, and metacognition
blocks.text:
A cognitive system comprises interacting components rather than one isolated method. Its architecture connects percepts from the environment to actions. Reaction supplies a direct mapping, such as an immediate response to an event. Deliberation uses knowledge through reasoning, learning, and memory. Metacognition reasons about the agent’s own processes, such as noticing that a strategy is failing and changing how to reason.

These are roles, not a mandatory serial pipeline. An agent can react without first performing an explicit plan; deliberation and monitoring can also influence behavior. Changing an estimate of the external world is object-level reasoning. Evaluating or changing the method used to produce that estimate is meta-level reasoning. That distinction will return in the later lessons on mistakes and meta-reasoning.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: The course’s unit of explanation is a knowledgeable cognitive agent: a representation and reasoning process situated within memory, learning, action, and monitoring. The recurring question is how these components achieve useful behavior despite limited resources.

blocks.title: What the course is trying to teach
blocks.text:
The goals connect core KBAI methods, cognitive architectures, common problem-solving tasks, and cognitive science. The outcomes are more than remembering names: design, implement, evaluate, and describe an agent; apply methods to practical problems; and relate computational accounts to cognition.

The book teaches through examples, doing, reflection, collaboration, and teaching. Its worked examples make a mechanism inspectable: what is represented, what operations are available, and why an answer follows. The ebook describes historical assessments, so use the Fall 2026 syllabus for current ARC-AGI work, deadlines, and exam scopes. The learning ideas remain relevant; the old Raven project instructions are not current submission requirements.

blocks.title: Computational psychometrics and visual analogy
blocks.text:
Psychometrics concerns measuring human intelligence, aptitude, and knowledge. Computational psychometrics builds agents that can attempt the same kinds of tests and uses their behavior to investigate cognition. The book’s Raven’s Progressive Matrices examples ask the solver to infer relationships among visual panels and identify a fitting completion.

In a simple A-to-B, C-to-D analogy, one strategy is to infer a transformation from A to B and apply it to C. Another is to consider candidate completions and test whether their relationships fit. The examples deliberately become more ambiguous: what looks like removing one shape could also be removing another and enlarging the remaining shape. The representation and the available alternatives affect which explanation is plausible.

blocks.title: From pair transformations to matrix relationships
blocks.text:
Larger matrices require consistency across more than one pair. The solver can examine rows, columns, and other relationships, distinguishing properties of individual objects from arrangements across panels. Some examples depend on a recurring set of features; others depend on the order of figures. A strategy that worked on an earlier pattern need not explain the next one.

The discussion contrasts inducing relationships before selecting a completion with inserting candidates and testing the resulting matrix. Equal answers do not establish equal reasoning processes. The purpose of the examples is to reveal these choices, not to treat all visual problems as one memorized transformation.

citations.section: Principles of CS7637; The Cognitive Connection

blocks.title: Seven ideas that recur throughout KBAI
blocks.text:
Agents represent and organize knowledge to guide reasoning. Learning is often incremental. Reasoning uses expectations from knowledge as well as incoming data: it is top-down, not only bottom-up. Agents match methods to tasks rather than using one method for everything.

Agents use heuristics to seek good-enough solutions under resource limits; they exploit recurring patterns; and reasoning, learning, and memory support and constrain one another. These principles connect the later lessons. For example, case retrieval exploits recurrence, frames guide expectations, and an impasse can create a learning need.

The cognitive connection goes in both directions: hypotheses about human problem solving inform agent designs, and explicit agent mechanisms suggest hypotheses about human cognition. Comparing errors as well as successes can be informative. Success on a restricted test alone is not a complete account of intelligence or proof of a human-like internal process.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: A useful agent explanation connects the task, representation, reasoning choices, and evidence from evaluation. Visual analogy is a recurring vehicle for that explanation, while the seven principles provide the course’s broader organizing thread.

chapters.title: Semantic Networks
chapters.summary: Semantic networks make objects and relationships explicit, supporting state-space search and comparison of transformations. Their usefulness depends on the task and chosen abstraction.

citations.section: Representations; Introduction to Semantic Networks; Structure of Semantic Networks

blocks.title: Representation is a language plus knowledge content
blocks.text:
A knowledge representation has a language and knowledge expressed in that language. Its lexicon supplies the vocabulary, its structure says how elements can be combined, and its semantics determines what those combinations mean for inference. A semantic network uses nodes and directed, labeled links to represent objects and relationships.

In the visual example, nodes represent a circle, a diamond, and a dot; links describe relations such as inside and above. Links between representations of successive panels express transformations such as unchanged, expanded, or deleted. A dummy endpoint can record a deleted object rather than pretending it still exists. A consistent vocabulary is essential: two networks cannot be compared reliably if the same relation is encoded differently without an explicit interpretation.

blocks.title: What makes a representation useful?
blocks.text:
A useful representation exposes the information and constraints needed for the task, at an appropriate level of abstraction. It should be understandable, concise without losing necessary information, and computable: the intended inferences must be possible over it.

The nutritional-label discussion illustrates the tradeoff. A label provides useful quantities, but may omit relationships among them and include information irrelevant to a particular reader. Completeness is therefore relative to the inferences a task requires, not a demand to encode every detail of the world. Omitting irrelevant visual detail can simplify an analogy, while omitting the relevant inside relation would make the desired comparison harder.

blocks.title: The same notation can represent a state space
blocks.text:
In the guards-and-prisoners problem, each node represents a whole state: numbers on each bank and the boat’s location. An edge represents a crossing. The boat carries one or two people and cannot travel alone; a bank with guards cannot have more prisoners than guards. These conditions distinguish legal from illegal successors.

Explicit state descriptions also reveal repeated states. If two sequences reach the same arrangement and boat location, their future possibilities need not be represented as unrelated situations. Identifying that repetition exposes loops that are easy to miss when solving informally. The network provides the representation; a reasoning process must still decide which states to generate, reject, or explore.

citations.section: Represent Reason for Analogy Problems; Exercise Represent Reason for Ravens; Choosing Matches by Weights; Connections

blocks.title: Compare relationships, then resolve ambiguous matches
blocks.text:
To compare A-to-B with C-to-a-candidate, compare the represented object relations and transformations. A candidate may preserve the spatial structure yet fail to reproduce an expansion, so a partial match is not the same as an exact match. Correspondence is also a problem: which object in one situation plays the role of which object in another?

When more than one transformation fits, weighted matching expresses a preference. The book’s illustrative scale gives a higher weight to an easier or more similar transformation, not a larger cost. Deleting one object while leaving another unchanged can score differently from deleting one and expanding another. Those weights explain a preference under the chosen metric; they do not make the ambiguous observation uniquely determine a transformation. This distinction returns in retrieval and analogical reasoning.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Semantic networks make relationships available to computation. State-space edges encode actions; analogy links encode spatial relations and transformations. Neither the notation nor a similarity score eliminates the need for an explicit reasoning method.

chapters.title: Generate & Test
chapters.summary: Generate and test separates proposing candidates from judging them. Knowledge can improve either side, while abstraction and repeated-state detection control wasted search.

citations.section: Preview; Guards and Prisoners

blocks.title: Generate a possibility; test whether it survives
blocks.text:
Generate and test is a general problem-solving method for situations where the agent cannot directly derive a guaranteed solution. The generator proposes possible solutions or successor states; the tester evaluates them against relevant requirements. The surviving possibilities support further search or a candidate answer.

The lesson reuses guards and prisoners. A simple generator proposes crossings, while a simple tester removes states that violate the bank-safety rule. This separates the representation from its use: a semantic network describes states and transitions, but does not itself explain which candidates an agent produces or rejects.

citations.section: Exercise Generate and Test II; Dumb Generators, Dumb Testers; Smart Testers

blocks.title: Legal does not mean productive
blocks.text:
A tester that checks only legality can retain repeated states, including returns to the initial state. Repeating expansion without recognizing equivalence creates a large search tree even in a small world. This is the lesson’s combinatorial-explosion problem: many generated paths need not correspond to genuinely new states.

A smarter tester checks whether a state has already been visited and can dismiss repeated states as well as illegal ones. Equivalent states can be merged in the representation. A branch with no remaining productive successor need not be mistaken for progress merely because its current state is legal. The representation must include all relevant state information, including the boat location, for that comparison to be meaningful.

blocks.title: Put knowledge in the generator, tester, or both
blocks.text:
Instead of generating a repeated or illegal state and rejecting it afterward, a smarter generator can avoid proposing it. The example of sending a lone person to an empty bank illustrates an unproductive return: the only next crossing undoes the move. Knowledge of that situation can prevent generation or support rejection.

The division of responsibility is a design choice. A richer generator may save testing work; a richer tester may keep generation simple. “Smart” here means endowed with relevant knowledge or discrimination, not a different kind of intelligence. Either way, broad generation without useful knowledge can be expensive, and rejection rules must preserve possibilities needed for a solution.

blocks.title: The representation determines the candidate space
blocks.text:
Visual transformations can vary continuously: an object can move many distances or expand by many amounts. If every pixel-level variation is a separate candidate, generation becomes unwieldy. A semantic representation can instead express the relevant relation, such as outside or expanded, without enumerating irrelevant geometric detail.

The generator can transfer a represented transformation to create a candidate completion, and the tester can compare it with the choices. This illustrates the coupling between representation and method: an abstraction makes certain distinctions available and suppresses others. The right abstraction depends on the task; ignoring a detail is helpful only when the solution does not require it.

chapters.title: Means-Ends Analysis
chapters.summary: Means-ends analysis chooses moves by their difference from a goal. Problem reduction breaks a goal into smaller problems; the blocks world shows why neither method alone resolves interacting goals.

citations.section: Exercise The Block Problem; State Spaces

blocks.title: State spaces: what is being searched?
blocks.text:
A state describes the current arrangement of the problem. An operator changes that arrangement. The state space contains the states reachable by applying operators repeatedly; solving the problem means finding a path from the initial state to a goal state. States are the nodes, and legal applications of operators are the directed edges. A path is therefore a sequence of actions, not just a list of pictures that resemble the goal.

The book uses a blocks world: initially A and B are on the table and C is on A; the goal is C on the table, B on C, and A on B. Only one block may move at a time, and a block with another block on it cannot move. These constraints determine which edges exist. Moving C to the table, then B onto C, then A onto B is a legal path. The next question is not whether that path exists, but how an agent selects it among other legal moves.

citations.section: Differences in State Spaces; Process of Means End Analysis

blocks.title: Means-ends analysis: use differences to select a move
blocks.text:
Means-ends analysis compares the current state with the goal, identifies differences, and chooses an applicable operator that brings the state closer to the goal. Reducing a difference is the end; applying an operator is the means. Here “distance” is an abstract measure of discrepancy, not physical distance on the table.

For the three-block example, count blocks whose support differs from the desired support. Initially there are three differences. Moving C to the table reduces the count to two; moving B onto C reduces it to one; moving A onto B reduces it to zero. This heuristic makes one successful path look attractive. But moving B onto C in the initial state also reduces the count to two. The heuristic alone does not resolve that tie. Do not infer a complete planning algorithm from this local selection rule: the lesson deliberately leaves some choices unresolved.

blocks.title: Why getting closer can trap the search
blocks.text:
The four-block example starts with B on C, D on B, and A on the table. The goal is the tower A on B on C on D, with D on the table. Moving D to the table achieves one missing relation; moving A onto B achieves another. Only C on D remains wrong, so the difference count is now one.

Yet C cannot move: B is on it, and A is on B. Achieving the remaining relation requires taking A off B and B off C, temporarily breaking relations that already match the final goal. A rule that insists on immediate discrepancy reduction cannot justify those preparatory moves. The book uses this obstacle to show that means-ends analysis may fail to make progress or enter loops. Its general applicability is not a guarantee of convergence, computational efficiency, or an optimal solution.

blocks.title: Problem reduction: solve subproblems, then recompose
blocks.text:
Problem reduction is a different idea: decompose a hard problem into smaller, easier problems, solve them, and combine the subsolutions. Knowledge helps identify a useful decomposition. For the tower, the final goal can be described as four subgoals: D on the table, C on D, B on C, and A on B.

The lesson focuses first on C on D while retaining D on the table. Relative to this smaller goal, the earlier matches A on B and B on C are no longer achievements that must be preserved at every step. Move A to the table, move B to the table to clear C, and then move C onto D. Finally put B on C and A on B to recompose the complete tower.

This explanation is not a claim that problem reduction automatically discovers that ordering. The book explicitly asks why C on D should be selected first and why placing A on D is a worse tied choice than placing A on the table. Subgoals can obstruct one another; decomposition alone does not solve their ordering or interaction. Planning returns to these unanswered questions later.

blocks.title: Why these are called weak methods
blocks.text:
The visual-analogy discussion combines the methods: find a transformation between two known panels, transfer it to a new panel, and compare the generated candidates with the choices. That is a decomposition; individual transformations can reduce differences; candidate comparison uses generate and test. A semantic network can support all three, so a complex problem need not use only one reasoning method.

“Weak” does not mean useless. These methods make relatively little use of domain knowledge, and their coupling to a particular knowledge representation is weak. That makes them broadly applicable, including in unfamiliar domains. Knowledge-intensive methods can exploit stronger domain structure to guide inference, but require that knowledge to be available. The historical Raven example illustrates this relationship; it is not the current ARC-AGI assignment specification.

chapters.title: Production Systems
chapters.summary: Production systems explain action selection through rules and changing working memory. In the book’s pitcher example, an unresolved choice creates an impasse, and chunking learns a production from episodic knowledge.

citations.section: Function of a Cognitive Architecture; Levels of Cognitive Architectures; Assumptions of Cognitive Architectures; Architecture Content Behavior

blocks.title: From perceptual history to action
blocks.text:
A cognitive agent can be described as mapping its perceptual history to an action. A cognitive architecture explains the mechanisms that make that mapping possible. The baseball pitcher is the running example: observations about the game and the goal of escaping the inning must lead to an action such as walking a batter or throwing a particular pitch.

The book distinguishes three levels of explanation. The task/knowledge level says what decision is required and what knowledge is available. The algorithm/symbol level says how that knowledge is represented and manipulated. The hardware level says how those processes are implemented. These are complementary descriptions: knowing the task does not specify the algorithm, and naming the hardware does not explain the knowledge used.

The architecture discussion assumes goal-directed agents in rich, changing environments. They use symbolic abstractions of world knowledge, adapt behavior to circumstances, and learn from experience. “Architecture + content = behavior” captures the central design idea: holding the architecture fixed while changing its knowledge content can produce different behavior. It does not make the content or its adequacy irrelevant.

citations.section: A Cognitive Architecture for Production Systems; Return to the Pitcher; Putting Content in the Architecture

blocks.title: Working memory and three kinds of long-term knowledge
blocks.text:
The lesson introduces SOAR as a cognitive architecture and concentrates on its deliberative role. Working memory holds the current represented situation and goals: the inning, occupied bases, batter, and goal in the pitcher example. These are feature-value descriptions, not the world itself.

Long-term memory includes procedural knowledge (how to do something), semantic knowledge (general concepts and models), and episodic knowledge (particular past events). Production rules represent procedural knowledge as conditions and consequences: if the antecedent matches, establish its consequent. Goals and observations can both occur in the conditions. Working memory supplies the current content against which rules are matched; episodic memory will later supply experience for learning. These roles are not interchangeable.

citations.section: Bringing in Memory; Exercise Production System in Action I; Exercise Production System in Action II

blocks.title: Rules change working memory, enabling further rules
blocks.text:
In the first pitcher situation, there are two outs, runners on second and third, and no runner on first. A matching rule suggests the goal of intentionally walking the batter. A further rule suggests the intentional-walk operator. The execution rule can then send the single selected operator to the motor system and record the action in working memory. Rule application can establish an intermediate goal, not merely trigger an immediate physical action.

After the walk, first base is occupied too. The production rules have not changed, but working memory has. A different rule now establishes the goal of getting the next batter out by pitching. With the right-handed batter in the example, the rules suggest a curve ball and the single-operator execution condition is satisfied.

This is a continuing interaction: matching rules establish consequences, consequences change working memory, and the new contents enable other rules. Working memory changes rapidly as the situation and intermediate conclusions change; long-term knowledge is more persistent. The changed decision after the walk is reasoning with new state information, not yet learning a new rule.

blocks.title: An impasse is a missing decision, not a chosen action
blocks.text:
Now the opposing team substitutes a left-handed batter. The same procedural knowledge suggests both a curve-ball operator and a fast-ball operator. The rule that executes an action requires exactly one selected operator, so it cannot fire. The system has reached an impasse: it cannot decide between competing actions. The book also allows an impasse when insufficient knowledge prevents a decision.

The important distinction is between having applicable rules and having enough knowledge to settle the action. This example does not say to execute both pitches or arbitrarily take the first rule. The architectural response is to seek knowledge that can resolve the impasse.

blocks.title: Chunking: use an episode to learn a production
blocks.text:
Episodic memory contains a previous encounter with the same batter, Parra: a fast ball resulted in a home run. Given the current goal of avoiding that outcome, the lesson’s learning process encapsulates relevant knowledge from the episode in a production: when two operators are suggested, one is a fast ball, and the batter is Parra, dismiss the fast-ball operator. This is the example of chunking.

The learned rule becomes procedural knowledge. Applying it in the current situation leaves the curve-ball operator as the sole suggestion, so the existing execution rule can fire. The architecture is unchanged; its content has changed. This is the learning step, distinct from the earlier working-memory changes.

The reasoning failure determines why and when to learn (resolve the impasse), what to learn (a deciding rule), and where to look (relevant episodic evidence); only then does the account specify how to learn it. Thus reasoning, memory, and learning form one connected explanation. This is the book’s illustrative model of decision making, not statistical proof that a fast ball always fails against that batter. Its cognitive connection discusses production systems as models of human behavior in restricted tasks, not a complete model of all human cognition.

chapters.title: Frames
chapters.summary: Frames organize stereotypical situations into slots and fillers. Defaults, inheritance, and linked frames let prior knowledge guide interpretation without making every expectation a fact.

citations.section: Exercise Ashok Ate a Frog; How do we make sense of a sentence; Exercise Making sense of a sentence

blocks.title: Slots describe what to expect; fillers describe this instance
blocks.text:
A frame is a structured representation of a stereotypical object, situation, or event. Slots describe the relevant attributes or roles; fillers supply values. For the eating frame, slots include the eater, what is eaten, location, time, and possible utensils. Different eating sentences instantiate the same structure with different fillers.

“Ashok ate a frog” supplies an eater and an object but not every detail a reader infers. The frame supplies expectations about eating, including possible default values for the object’s location afterward. A filler obtained from the sentence and a default inferred from prior knowledge have different evidential status. The book’s guessed mood after eating illustrates that expectations can be wrong, not that eating always makes someone happy.

blocks.title: Link frames, inherit structure, and override defaults
blocks.text:
A filler can point to another frame rather than be a simple value. An eating-event frame can link to a person frame with food preferences and to a restaurant frame with its location. Connecting frames combines knowledge from several sentences and supports discourse-level interpretation.

The three central properties are stereotypes, defaults with exceptions, and inheritance. A subclass or instance can inherit slots and values from a more general frame and add or override information. This avoids restating everything, but exceptions must be managed. Stereotypes can also vary with culture and context. A default provides a defeasible expectation, not a logical necessity that overrides contrary evidence.

citations.section: Frames and Semantic Nets; Frames and Production Systems

blocks.title: Frames connect earlier representations
blocks.text:
The same object-and-relation information in a semantic network can be expressed in frames. A diamond’s frame can have an inside slot whose filler refers to a circle’s frame. The drawing of an edge and the named slot are different notations for a represented relationship.

The feature-value working memory in the production-system lesson can also be understood as frame-like structure. An input cue such as an eating verb retrieves a relevant frame from semantic memory. Its slots guide attention to expected information; the incoming sentence then supplies particular fillers. This connects representation with memory and processing rather than leaving the frame as a static form.

citations.section: Exercise Frames Complex Understanding; The Cognitive Connection

blocks.title: Understanding combines top-down expectation and bottom-up input
blocks.text:
The earthquake story illustrates the process: retrieve an earthquake frame, look for relevant roles such as location and magnitude, then fill them from the story. The frame provides top-down expectations, while the actual wording provides bottom-up evidence.

A frame cannot infer everything merely because a slot exists. In the story, connecting the place described in the text with a broader geographical location needs additional knowledge; the frame alone does not supply that reasoning. Frames make useful information organized and accessible, but other reasoning methods must interpret relationships, resolve missing information, and handle exceptions.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Frames explain how structured prior knowledge helps make sense of incomplete input. Their strength is organized expectation; their limitation is that defaults, inherited values, and open slots do not by themselves establish every missing fact.

chapters.title: Learning by Recording Cases
chapters.summary: Learning by recording cases stores experiences for direct reuse. Nearest-neighbor retrieval makes similarity explicit, but a close case is not necessarily a solution that can be reused unchanged.

citations.section: Exercise Block World I; Learning by Recording Cases

blocks.title: A case encapsulates an experience
blocks.text:
A case records a past situation together with its solution or outcome. Learning by recording cases retains those experiences instead of immediately abstracting a general rule. A new problem acts as a probe into memory; retrieve a similar case and reuse its solution.

The colored-block example predicts a new block’s color from a remembered block of similar shape and size. Familiar routines such as tying shoelaces illustrate how memory can reduce the need to reason from scratch. This is direct reuse: it is distinct from adapting a solution to a different problem, which the next lesson adds.

citations.section: Case Retrieval by Nearest Neighbor; Exercise Retrieval by Nearest Neighbor

blocks.title: Operationalize “most similar” with a distance
blocks.text:
Represent the stored blocks and the new block by width and height in the same feature space. Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. The nearest neighbor is the recorded case with the smallest distance to the new problem under that representation.

The calculation makes the comparison reproducible, but the representation determines what similarity means. Width and height support the lesson’s example; they do not show that any similarly shaped object must have the same color. Retrieval chooses a case under the selected metric, not a guarantee that its answer is correct.

citations.section: Exercise Recording Cases in Real Life; Nearest Neighbor for Complex Problems; Nearest Neighbor in k-Dimensional Space

blocks.title: A route has both an origin and a destination
blocks.text:
The route example makes one-feature similarity inadequate. A stored route can start close to the new origin but finish far from the requested destination; another can finish close but start far away. Comparing only either endpoint selects a misleading case.

The lesson represents both endpoints by coordinates, making a four-dimensional comparison. More generally, compare a case and problem in k-dimensional space by summing squared differences across the relevant coordinates. The ebook calls this KNN while discussing k dimensions; it does not teach a majority vote over k retrieved neighbors here. Keep the dimensionality of the representation separate from the number of neighbors selected.

blocks.title: Retrieval is useful even when direct reuse fails
blocks.text:
High-dimensional descriptions can make similarity harder to compute or interpret. Some cases also require qualitative features rather than numerical coordinates. Most importantly, a nearby route need not start and end at exactly the new problem’s locations, so copying it unchanged may fail.

This motivates case-based reasoning: alternative retrieval organizations, adaptation, and evaluation. The cognitive connection emphasizes recurring problems and the contribution of memory to intelligence. Recording cases does not remove reasoning; it shifts the balance toward remembered experience where that experience is relevant.

chapters.title: Case-Based Reasoning
chapters.summary: Case-based reasoning extends case retrieval with adaptation, evaluation, and selective storage. Memory organization and feedback determine whether experience can solve a new problem.

citations.section: Recording Cases to Case-Based Reasoning; Assumptions of Case-Based Reasoning

blocks.title: Retrieve, adapt, evaluate, store
blocks.text:
A similar case may be useful without being a complete solution. The route retrieved in the previous lesson has different endpoints from the new request. Case-based reasoning retrieves that experience, adapts its solution, evaluates the resulting candidate, and stores useful new experience.

The method assumes recurring problem patterns and that similar problems often have similar solutions. Neither is universal: fastening a shoe with laces and fastening one with Velcro are similar goals with different mechanisms. Retrieval proposes a starting point, not evidence that adaptation will be small or successful.

citations.section: Case Adaptation; Case Adaptation by Model of the World; Case Adaptation by Recursive Reasoning; Case Adaptation by Rules

blocks.title: Three ways to adapt an old solution
blocks.text:
Model-based adaptation uses knowledge of how the world works. In the route example, a map supplies a connection from the old route’s endpoint to the new destination. The case contributes much of the path; the model supplies the missing change.

Recursive case-based adaptation turns an unsolved part into another retrieval problem. Combine a home-to-office case with an office-to-restaurant case to solve home-to-restaurant. The subsolutions must fit together; retrieving two cases is not enough without a valid composition.

Rule-based adaptation applies a heuristic such as reversing a route to return home. A rule of thumb may work often but fail on one-way streets. This is why adaptation creates a candidate for evaluation rather than automatically a correct answer. The three methods use different knowledge sources: a world model, other cases, or adaptation rules.

citations.section: Case Evaluation; Case Storage; Case Storage by Index

blocks.title: Evaluate before treating a candidate as success
blocks.text:
Evaluation asks whether the adapted solution meets the new problem’s requirements. Simulation, execution, prototyping, or critique can provide evidence, depending on the domain and cost of failure. The reversed route may fail because a turn is prohibited, even though its derivation looked plausible.

A new problem and evaluated solution can become a case. Storage must also make later retrieval possible. An index records features useful for finding the case, such as route origin, destination, speed, or scenic quality. The features useful for retrieval depend on the future task, so indexing is part of the reasoning design, not just archiving a transcript.

citations.section: Case Storage by Discrimination Tree; Exercise Storage by Discrimin Tree I; Exercise Storage by Discrimin Tree II; Case Retrieval Revisited

blocks.title: Discrimination trees organize cases by questions
blocks.text:
A discrimination tree places cases at leaves and feature questions at internal nodes. Answers select branches. To store a new case, follow its answers; if it reaches a leaf shared with an existing case, add a question that separates them. To retrieve, use the new problem’s features to follow the same organization.

The navigation example asks questions about origin coordinates. A question can prune a whole branch instead of comparing every case in a table. The tree need not be binary, and its usefulness depends on discriminating questions and the selected indices. This retrieval organization is distinct from adapting whatever case it returns.

citations.section: Advanced Case-Based Reasoning; Wrap Up

blocks.title: The process can loop, and storage has a utility cost
blocks.text:
Evaluation failure can return to adaptation or to retrieval of a different case. An exact match can skip adaptation but still needs evaluation. A failed case can be worth storing because it warns of a future failure; a redundant successful case may add little value.

The utility problem is that accumulating cases can make retrieval less efficient. Selective storage seeks experience that expands useful coverage, not simply a larger library. The cycle therefore connects learning, memory, and reasoning: learn experience, organize and retrieve it, then reason about adapting and testing it.

chapters.title: Incremental Concept Learning
chapters.summary: Incremental concept learning revises a concept from labeled examples. Generalization includes missed positives; specialization excludes mistaken negatives; heuristics and background knowledge guide the change.

citations.section: Exercise Identifying a Foo I; Exercise Identifying a Foo II; Exercise Identifying a Foo III; Incremental Concept Learning

blocks.title: Learn a concept, not just another case
blocks.text:
The agent receives examples one at a time, labeled positive or negative. Unlike recording raw cases for later reuse, it abstracts a concept description. That description must cover positive examples and exclude negative ones.

For each new example, compare its label with whether the current concept covers it. A covered positive or excluded negative requires no change. A missed positive calls for generalization; a covered negative calls for specialization. The learner must still respect earlier examples. Learning from a small sequence is underdetermined: many possible changes can fit the evidence, so the representation, example order, and background knowledge matter.

blocks.title: The arch example revises relationships
blocks.text:
The first arch example is variabilized: replace particular brick names with variables or categories while retaining their relationships. A later positive example lacks an incidental relationship in the initial description, so drop-link removes that constraint to include both examples.

A negative example lacking the required support relation motivates require-link: mark that relation as necessary. Another negative example has the supporting blocks touching, motivating forbid-link: exclude that relationship. These are different changes. Dropping a link loosens a description, requiring one tightens it, and forbidding one explicitly rules out its presence. A near miss is informative because it differs from a positive structure in a revealing way.

blocks.title: Generalization can change categories or value ranges
blocks.text:
A positive arch with a wedge where the description allowed only a brick can be included by enlarge-set: allow brick or wedge. If background knowledge says both are kinds of block, climb-tree generalizes to their shared category. These are not the same inference: the shared category comes from additional knowledge.

Close-interval extends an allowed continuous range to cover observed values, such as including a larger dog after seeing only small ones. The heuristics constrain a large space of possible revisions; they do not prove that an arbitrary generalization is the intended concept. Preserve the distinction between what the examples show and what background knowledge licenses.

citations.section: An Alternative Visualization; Final Concept of a Foo; The Cognitive Connection

blocks.title: The learned definition is limited by the evidence
blocks.text:
The repeated foo examples make the learner’s decisions inspectable: variabilize, compare structures, revise for labeled differences, and use a supplied category hierarchy where available. The final definition need not contain required links that the input sequence never justified, nor generalizations that the background knowledge never supplied.

Overgeneralization includes things that should be excluded; overspecialization excludes things that should be included. Labels and carefully contrasting examples help repair both, but the resulting concept remains relative to the represented features and available evidence. An example that the representation cannot distinguish cannot teach the missing distinction by itself.

chapters.title: Classification
chapters.summary: Classification organizes percepts into useful concepts for action. Concept hierarchies guide search, while axiomatic, prototype, and exemplar concepts require different kinds of representation and inference.

citations.section: Classifying Birds; The Challenge of Classification; Equivalence Classes

blocks.title: Classification compresses the action-selection problem
blocks.text:
Classification maps sets of percepts into concepts or equivalence classes. Instead of choosing an action separately for every possible combination of observed features, an agent groups situations that can be treated alike for the task. This can make action selection manageable.

The bird examples show why selecting features matters: the ability to fly does not characterize every bird, since penguins and ostriches provide counterexamples. An equivalence class is useful relative to what the agent needs to do. It does not mean every member is identical in every property. Learning a concept and using it to classify are related but distinct tasks.

blocks.title: Establish and refine through a concept hierarchy
blocks.text:
Organize concepts into superclasses and subclasses. A top-down establish-and-refine process first determines a broad category, then considers its finer distinctions. The animal example proceeds toward vertebrate, bird, and a particular kind of bird.

The organization guides attention: size may not distinguish bird from mammal, but can matter when separating examples within birds. Shared subclass properties can inform a superclass where the concept supports such a definition. The book cautions that this works for some formal concepts, not every everyday concept. Organization controls the reasoning sequence rather than merely arranging labels for display.

blocks.title: Three kinds of concept do not have the same definition
blocks.text:
An axiomatic concept has explicit necessary and sufficient conditions, as with the geometrical definition of a circle. Classification can test those conditions. A prototype concept instead has typical properties that may admit exceptions. The chair example uses a frame with defaults; a stool can override the expected back without ceasing to fit the broader category in the example.

An exemplar concept is conveyed through examples without an agreed necessary-and-sufficient or typical-property definition, illustrated by beauty. Such concepts can depend on culture or individuals. A frame is a representation form; a prototype is a kind of concept content. Confusing these levels would make every frame appear to be a prototype classifier and every everyday concept appear formally definable.

blocks.text:

The lesson’s point is method-task fit, not that this illustration guarantees stock-market prediction. Different concept types and organizations afford different methods: formal conditions, prototypes with exceptions, or remembered exemplars. Classification is therefore a family of reasoning tasks rather than one universal feature checklist.

chapters.title: Logic
chapters.summary: Logic separates formal knowledge from inference. Connectives, truth-preserving rewrites, quantifiers, and resolution show precisely why a conclusion follows from stated premises.

citations.section: Why do we need formal logic; Predicates; Conjunctions and Disjunctions; Implies

blocks.title: A knowledge base and an inference engine have different jobs
blocks.text:
A logical agent has a knowledge base of statements and an inference engine that applies rules to derive conclusions. Formal notation makes the assertions and steps precise. A predicate expresses a property or relation; connectives form compound statements using not, and, or, and implication.

Conjunction requires both components, disjunction allows either or both, and negation reverses a truth value. An implication states that when its antecedent holds its consequent must hold. Soundness means deriving only conclusions supported by the premises; completeness means the inference system can derive every entailed conclusion within the relevant logic. Neither property makes incorrect premises into true statements about the world, nor guarantees an inexpensive search.

citations.section: Truth Tables; Exercise Commutative Property; Exercise Distributive Property; Exercise Associative Property; Exercise de Morgans Law; Truth of Implications; Implication Elimination

blocks.title: Truth tables justify rewrites
blocks.text:
A truth table enumerates assignments to simple statements and evaluates a compound statement. Two expressions are equivalent when their truth values agree on every assignment. This justifies changing an expression’s form without changing what it asserts.

And and or are commutative and associative. Distribution moves between conjunctions and disjunctions in equivalent forms. De Morgan’s laws turn not(A and B) into not A or not B, and not(A or B) into not A and not B. Implication elimination rewrites A implies B as not A or B. The implication is false only when A is true and B is false; a false antecedent does not establish B as a fact. These rewrites prepare statements for systematic inference.

blocks.title: Valid inference is not guessing the converse
blocks.text:
Modus ponens uses A implies B together with A to infer B. Modus tollens uses A implies B together with not B to infer not A. The bird example instantiates an asserted rule about feathers and an observed fact about Harry to derive the asserted classification.

Knowing B does not in general license A, and knowing not A does not license not B. The consequent might hold for another reason. A proof explains what follows from a particular knowledge base; it does not replace checking whether that knowledge base correctly models the domain.

blocks.title: Variables and quantifiers express scope
blocks.text:
Propositional statements concern fixed assertions. First-order logic introduces variables within predicates and quantifiers that specify their scope. A universal quantifier says a statement holds for every value in the specified domain; an existential quantifier says it holds for at least one.

A general animal rule can be written once with a universally quantified variable instead of separately for every named animal. An existential claim must not be silently strengthened into a universal one. The lesson introduces this language, then returns to propositional examples for resolution. It does not provide a full treatment of first-order unification or Skolemization.

citations.section: A Simple Proof; A More Complex Proof; Exercise Proof I; Exercise Proof II; Exercise Proof III; Exercise Proof IV; Exercise Proof V; Exercise Proof VI

blocks.title: Resolution proves by refuting the negated conclusion
blocks.text:
Convert the knowledge base to conjunctive normal form (CNF): a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. A literal is an atom or its negation; a single literal is also a clause. Eliminate implications, move negations inward using De Morgan’s laws, and distribute where required. Add the negation of the conclusion you want to establish.

Resolution combines two clauses containing complementary literals. Resolving A or B with not A or C yields B or C: if both original clauses hold, the remaining alternatives must hold. The empty clause has no surviving alternative and represents contradiction. If the knowledge base plus the negated goal yields that contradiction, the goal is entailed by the knowledge base.

The assembly-line robot first uses “not can-move implies not liftable” and observes “not can-move.” In CNF the rule is “can-move or not liftable.” To prove not liftable, temporarily add liftable. Resolve it against not liftable in the rule to derive can-move; resolve that against the observed not can-move to obtain the empty clause. In the longer example, the rule also requires battery-full: its CNF clause is “can-move or not battery-full or not liftable.” Resolving with liftable, battery-full, and not can-move again produces contradiction.

The bird proof demonstrates the same process with wings and fur. Proof search still requires choosing clauses and may be costly; one unfinished branch without a contradiction is not proof that the goal is false. Entailment is relative to the premises, and inconsistent premises themselves undermine a useful account of the world.

chapters.title: Planning
chapters.summary: Planning represents states, goals, and action conditions explicitly, then coordinates subplans so achieving one goal does not prevent another.

citations.section: Painting a Ceiling; States; Operators; Exercise Operators; Planning and State Spaces

blocks.title: States, goals, and operators make action reasoning precise
blocks.text:
A state specifies assertions about the world; a goal specifies assertions to achieve. An operator has preconditions that must hold before it applies and postconditions describing its effects. Assertions not changed by an operator can persist to the next state. This makes a plan a checkable sequence, not merely an informal intention.

The robot must paint both a ceiling and a ladder. Climbing requires the robot on the floor and a dry ladder; painting the ceiling requires the robot on the ladder. Painting the ladder leaves it wet. The printed operators distinguish painted from dry: achieving the painted-ladder goal can remove the dry-ladder condition needed for climbing. Positive preconditions are a convention of the illustrated planning notation, not a universal law that planning can never use negative conditions.

citations.section: Planning; Partial Order Planning; Partial Planning; Detecting Conflicts; Open Preconditions

blocks.title: Detect goal clobbering and impose the needed order
blocks.text:
A linear treatment can choose to paint the ladder first because that immediately achieves one goal, then discover that the wet ladder prevents climbing to paint the ceiling. The plan for one goal clobbers a condition required by another.

The lesson constructs subplans, compares their effects and required conditions, and resolves conflicts by promoting or demoting their order. Paint the ceiling before painting the ladder. An open precondition is a required condition not yet supported in the combined plan: after painting the ceiling, the robot must descend to establish being on the floor before painting the ladder. Adding that action joins the subplans. Partial-order planning imposes necessary dependencies rather than assuming all goals can be achieved independently in any order.

blocks.title: The blocks-world conflict is now explicit
blocks.text:
Moving x onto y requires both blocks clear in the illustrated world. Putting A on B makes B no longer clear, so it interferes with moving B onto C. Putting B on C similarly interferes with moving C onto D. Comparing those effects with the next action’s preconditions exposes the ordering problem left open by means-ends analysis and problem reduction.

The goal-supporting tower must therefore be built from the bottom upward after necessary clearing moves. This is not because “bottom upward” is an unexplained preference: it follows from the represented clear conditions and the effects of stacking. The source’s planning mechanism turns that tacit reasoning into explicit dependencies.

blocks.title: Hierarchical plans use knowledge at several levels
blocks.text:
A long sequence of low-level block moves can be grouped into macro operators such as unstack and stack-ascending. A macro has conditions and a decomposition into lower-level actions. Planning at the higher level reduces the apparent search space; expanding the macro supplies the detailed operations.

A hierarchical task network represents those task decompositions. The power comes from additional knowledge about useful abstractions and how to realize them, not merely renaming a long action list. Hierarchical planning and partial ordering address different concerns: abstraction organizes levels of a plan, while ordering resolves dependencies and conflicts among actions.

blocks.text: Planning adds explicit action conditions and inter-goal dependencies to goal-directed search. Partial ordering protects necessary conditions; hierarchical decomposition exploits knowledge about useful subplans.

chapters.title: Understanding
chapters.summary: Understanding uses thematic-role frames, grammatical cues, and background categories to interpret events and disambiguate meanings.

citations.section: The Earthquake Report; Thematic Role Systems

blocks.title: Meaning is organized around an event and its roles
blocks.text:
A thematic-role system is a frame system for an action or event. It organizes participants by semantic roles such as agent, object, beneficiary, instrument, source, destination, and conveyance. These are different from lexical categories such as noun and verb or syntactic categories such as noun phrase.

In the pancake example, the maker is the agent, pancakes the object, the person they are made for the beneficiary, and the griddle the instrument. The representation supports questions about who did what for whom. The lesson treats meaningful inferences as evidence of understanding, while reminding us that expectations inferred from an event are not necessarily explicit statements in the sentence.

citations.section: Constraints; Resolving Ambiguity in Prepositions

blocks.title: Prepositions constrain a role without uniquely deciding it
blocks.text:
The preposition by can indicate an agent, a conveyance, or a location. Its presence narrows possible roles, but does not choose one alone. Background knowledge about people, trains, and places helps distinguish “written by a person,” “travel by train,” and “standing by a statue.”

An ontology supplies categories for that background knowledge. Lexical and structural cues act as probes into memory; retrieved role knowledge then generates top-down expectations. Understanding combines that knowledge with the actual words rather than proceeding only from syntax or only from an unconstrained prior guess.

A word such as take has several meanings, with different thematic-role frames. “Took my blood pressure” calls for a measurement interpretation, while taking an object from someone supplies an object and source. Background categories rule out inappropriate interpretations; prepositions and particles such as from or over impose further constraints.

The agent activates candidate senses and tests whether their expected roles fit the sentence. A frame that cannot accommodate the known categories or required roles is discarded. The killing examples similarly distinguish people dying in an earthquake from proposals being rejected. A pun can deliberately satisfy more than one interpretation, so ambiguity is not always an error with one answer to recover.

chapters.summary: Commonsense reasoning represents related meanings with primitive actions and connects actions to implied events and state changes.

blocks.title: Different words can describe the same underlying action
blocks.text:
The earlier understanding lesson asked how one word can have different meanings. This lesson asks the converse: how different words can convey a similar event. Ate, consumed, and ingested can share an ingestion interpretation in an appropriate context, even if their connotations differ.

Primitive actions provide a common internal vocabulary for such interpretations. The book includes move-object, move-possession, ingest, propel, speak, and other primitives. Move-object concerns physical movement; move-possession concerns a transfer of possession. Their distinction matters: changing who has a book and moving a book through space are not identical descriptions. Each primitive has a frame of roles and relevant expectations.

Bottom-up cues trigger top-down expectations; lexical, syntactic, and semantic analysis cooperate. If a candidate primitive frame fits poorly, the agent may have to reconsider it rather than force every word into the wrong slots. This structured representation supports questions such as who now has an object and who had it before.

blocks.title: An action can be implied rather than named directly
blocks.text:
“Fertilized the field” can be interpreted through an implied movement of fertilizer onto the field, even though the sentence does not directly name the lower-level movement. Background knowledge supplies a decomposition that maps more readily to primitive actions.

Actions can have subactions and change states. A sentence may emphasize the event, its result, or an attitude toward it. The representation must distinguish what was performed from what state resulted or was desired. An inferred consequence depends on the modeled action and context; it must not be asserted merely because two sentences share a word.

blocks.title: Connect action frames and resultant states
blocks.text:
Sentences with multiple verbs can require multiple linked frames: deciding to act, communicating an instruction, performing an action, or enjoying an event are not one undifferentiated verb. Connections among action and state-change frames make the interpretation explicit.

The lesson’s cognitive connection extends beyond physical movement to goals, beliefs, and desires used in social interpretation. It is an introductory representation account, not a complete inventory of all commonsense knowledge. Scripts next combine primitive-event frames into longer, familiar sequences.

blocks.text: Primitive actions abstract across surface wording while linked frames represent roles, implied subevents, and consequences. The abstraction supports commonsense interpretation, but its inferences still require appropriate background knowledge.
