chapters.title: Scripts
chapters.summary: Scripts represent familiar, causally coherent sequences of events. They connect frames across a story and generate expectations that can be violated.

citations.section: Story Understanding for AI Agents; Visiting a Coffeehouse; Definition of Scripts; Parts of a Script

blocks.title: A script is structured knowledge about an event sequence
blocks.text:
A script captures a causally coherent set of events, not just one sentence or an unordered collection of facts. The coffeehouse example is understandable because the reader knows what typically follows arriving, ordering, paying, and receiving a drink. Some unstated events can be inferred from that familiar structure.

The six parts are entry conditions, results, props, roles, tracks, and scenes. Entry conditions describe when the script applies; results describe its expected outcome; props are involved objects; roles are participants; tracks are variations; scenes organize event sequences. These parts supply both a representation of a typical situation and expectations about its progression.

citations.section: Constructing a Script; Form vs Content

blocks.title: Instantiate scenes rather than treating the stereotype as the event
blocks.text:
The restaurant script describes roles such as customer and waiter, props such as menus and food, and scenes such as entering, ordering, eating, and paying. A particular visit fills those variables with particular people and objects. Primitive-action frames represent the component events within the scenes.

The general script and its current instance are distinct. The stored structure can help an agent choose what to do without constructing a new plan from scratch, but only where the situation fits the script. The restaurant sequence is a contextual stereotype, not a universal rule for every culture or establishment.

blocks.title: Surprise reveals a failed expectation or an unexpected event
blocks.text:
Waiting for a menu that never arrives is an expectation violation. Receiving a bill before ordering is an unexpected event. Both are recognizable because the script predicted a different progression. Identifying the scene where the mismatch occurs gives the agent a more specific problem than simply declaring the whole story confusing.

Tracks distinguish variations such as coffeehouse, fast food, and formal dining. Observed cues help classify the situation into the appropriate track. The agent may refine its choice as more evidence arrives rather than insist that every restaurant follow its first selected sequence.

blocks.title: Learning and using scripts are different tasks
blocks.text:
Learning a script abstracts recurring event structure; using one retrieves and instantiates that structure for a new situation. Frames and semantic networks provide representational components. Concept learning can distinguish tracks, planning can provide a sequence worth retaining, and commonsense primitives provide a vocabulary for the events.

Classification selects a suitable script; understanding interprets the current story; decomposition can locate an obstruction within a scene. The cognitive connection emphasizes the combination of top-down prediction and bottom-up correction. Fast routine understanding is possible because much structure is already stored, not because unfamiliar or exceptional events need no reasoning.

blocks.text: Scripts make longer stories understandable through stored event structure. They save repeated planning, but their predictions must remain responsive to the actual track and unexpected events.

chapters.title: Explanation-Based Learning
chapters.summary: Explanation-based learning abstracts relevant causal knowledge from known concepts and transfers it to explain a new instance.

citations.section: Exercise Transporting Soup; Example Retrieving a Cup; Concept Space; Prior Knowledge

blocks.title: Use prior knowledge to explain a novel use
blocks.text:
The soup and cup examples ask how an agent recognizes an unfamiliar object as suitable when its usual utensil is unavailable. Explanation-based learning does not simply collect many new examples or invent a concept from nothing. It connects existing conceptual knowledge to establish why the new instance satisfies a needed description.

Prior knowledge includes causal fragments: a brick is stable because it has a flat bottom; a bowl carries liquid because it is concave; a briefcase is liftable because it is light and has a handle; a glass enables drinking because it carries liquid and is liftable. These are the source’s simplified domain relationships. Incidental decoration or unrelated attributes need not participate in the explanation.

citations.section: Abstraction; Transfer

blocks.title: Abstract the causal relationship, then transfer it
blocks.text:
Abstraction replaces the particular source object with a variable or general object while retaining the relationship needed for the explanation. The useful knowledge from the bowl is not its name or contents, but the modeled connection from concavity to carrying liquid.

To show the new object is a cup under the given definition, work backward from stable and enables-drinking. Stability is supported by the flat-bottom fragment. Enabling drinking requires carrying liquid and being liftable, supported by the bowl and briefcase fragments. Their effects become conditions in the glass fragment. The agent composes those explanations and checks their conditions against the new object. This is goal-directed retrieval of relevant knowledge, not indiscriminate transfer of every property of a source.

The other cup conditions can be established, yet the complete mug explanation cannot be made from that knowledge alone.

The missing relationship identifies what additional knowledge is needed. Similar-sounding phrases are not automatically interchangeable predicates. This is a limitation and a learning opportunity: reasoning specifies a precise gap instead of filling it with an unsupported assertion.

chapters.title: Analogical Reasoning
chapters.summary: Analogical reasoning retrieves a source by meaningful similarity, maps corresponding roles, and transfers a relational pattern across domains before evaluation.

citations.section: Exercise Similarity Ratings; Cases Revisited; Need for Cross-Domain Analogy; Spectrum of Similarity

blocks.title: Similar objects and similar relationships are different evidence
blocks.text:
A woman climbing a ladder and a woman painting a ladder share objects but differ in the relevant relation. An ant climbing a wall shares less surface appearance but a relation of ascent. Analogical reasoning can use such relational similarity to understand a target problem through a familiar source, including across domains.

Recording cases and case-based reasoning are within-domain forms of reuse. Cross-domain analogy additionally needs to determine which different objects play corresponding roles. The textbook’s fortress-and-radiation thought experiment illustrates transfer of a convergence strategy through shared resource, obstacle, and goal relations. It is a cognitive-science example, not a medical treatment recommendation.

citations.section: Process of Analogical Reasoning; Analogical Retrieval; Three Types of Similarity

blocks.title: Retrieve by the kind of similarity that matters
blocks.text:
The described process has retrieval, mapping, transfer, evaluation, and storage. Retrieval must notice deeper relationships rather than rely only on object names, feature values, or counts. Higher-order relationships can connect the relations themselves, such as how an obstacle prevents a resource from achieving a goal.

Semantic similarity concerns concepts; pragmatic similarity concerns goals and other task-related considerations; structural similarity concerns relationships in the representations. These are not interchangeable measures. Different tasks or theories may weight them differently. Structural similarity is about representational organization, not just two objects having a similar physical outline.

citations.section: Analogical Mapping; Exercise Analogical Mapping; Analogical Transfer; Exercise Analogical Transfer

blocks.title: Map roles before transferring a solution
blocks.text:
Mapping solves the correspondence problem: what in the source matches what in the target? In the fortress example, the resource corresponds to the resource and the obstacle to the obstacle. Superficially matching two people would miss the goal structure. In the historical solar-system/atom model, center and revolving-object roles constrain a mapping that object properties alone leave ambiguous.

Transfer abstracts a source relationship or strategy and instantiates it using that mapping. It is selective, not a claim that the target inherits every source property. The atomic example is a simplified historical teaching model for correspondence, not a complete physical account of atoms. A convincing mapping can still propose an incorrect target solution, so evaluation remains necessary.

blocks.text:
The biologically inspired design discussion uses models of structure, behavior, and function, not merely visual resemblance. A water-walking organism supplies knowledge about how its structure achieves locomotion; mapping and transfer can proceed through these levels to a proposed robot design.

Compositional analogy can build up a transfer through related levels of a model. Compound analogy combines useful parts from multiple sources, as in the low-speed and high-speed swimming examples. Simulation or prototyping may reveal failure and send the process back to mapping, transfer, or retrieval. The target problem itself can evolve as a partial design exposes a new requirement. Common vocabulary, selecting relevant knowledge, and combining sources remain difficult questions rather than solved guarantees.

blocks.text: Analogy is a knowledge-guided transfer process, not resemblance as proof. Retrieval finds a promising source, mapping establishes roles, transfer proposes an answer, and evaluation determines whether it works.

chapters.title: Version Spaces
chapters.summary: Version spaces retain consistent concept hypotheses between specific and general boundaries. Identification trees offer another organization of labeled examples, trading incremental arrival for batch feature selection.

citations.section: Incremental Concept Learning Revisited; Abstract Version Spaces; Visualizing Version Spaces

blocks.title: Keep alternatives instead of committing to one description
blocks.text:
The earlier concept learner revised one current description using carefully informative examples and background knowledge. Version-space learning instead tracks possible descriptions consistent with the examples, bounded by specific and general models. It addresses how far to generalize when the order of examples is not controlled and background categories may be unavailable.

The specific side covers the observed positives as narrowly as the hypothesis form permits. The general side remains as broad as the evidence allows while excluding negatives. They are boundaries of the remaining possibilities, not a claim that one initial guess is already correct. Multiple alternatives can persist until later examples discriminate among them.

blocks.title: The meal example narrows both sides
blocks.text:
The book’s invented meal records use restaurant, meal, day, and cost with a positive or negative reaction label. The first positive record creates a specific description of that visit and a completely general alternative. A negative record specializes the general alternatives to exclude it without excluding the positive. A further positive generalizes the specific description and removes general alternatives that cannot cover it.

With the complete illustrated sequence, the surviving description is cheap meals at Sam’s. Intermediate hypotheses such as all meals at Sam’s remain until a discriminating example eliminates them. Pruning removes inconsistent models and redundant boundary models subsumed by retained ones. Negative examples must be excluded, not “included” as a damaged transcript sentence suggests. These are teaching data about hypothesis revision, not an actual allergy diagnosis.

blocks.title: Convergence depends on evidence and hypothesis form
blocks.text:
Informative positive and negative examples can bring the specific and general boundaries together. For the illustrated representable concept, the consistent final result does not depend on the order of those examples. A lack of discriminating evidence can leave several hypotheses; an insufficient description language can prevent a satisfactory concept from being represented at all.

The lesson notes that reactions to multiple combinations, such as different meals at different restaurants, can defeat the simple hypothesis form. More records do not repair an unexpressible distinction. More features and examples also demand more computation. Convergence therefore must not be read as an unconditional promise that any dataset eventually yields the true concept.

blocks.title: Identification trees choose features to separate labels
blocks.text:
An identification or decision tree organizes labeled examples by feature questions. The meal example first separates restaurants, then separates the remaining mixed group by cost, until leaves have a consistent label. The sunburn illustration compares feature orders that yield shorter or bushier trees on the given data.

Unlike incrementally adding a discrimination question when a new stored case collides with an old one, this discussion chooses questions with the batch of examples available. The tradeoff is up-front data versus a more economical classification tree for those examples. The examples illustrate feature selection; they do not prove a greedy question choice always constructs the globally optimal tree or that a training correlation is a causal law.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Version spaces make uncertainty among concept descriptions explicit. Decision trees organize discrimination differently. Both are constrained by the chosen features, labeled evidence, and representational capacity.

chapters.title: Constraint Propagation
chapters.summary: Constraint propagation uses local restrictions to seek globally compatible interpretations. Line labeling and grammar show how assigning one value constrains neighboring choices without always producing a unique answer.

citations.section: Exercise Recognizing 3D Figures; Exercise Gibberish Sentences; Constraint Propagation Defined

blocks.title: Variables, values, and constraints define interpretation
blocks.text:
Constraint propagation assigns values to variables so that relevant conditions are satisfied together. A local assignment can rule out choices elsewhere. The lesson’s recognition examples ask how a two-dimensional drawing can represent surfaces of a three-dimensional object, or how words can form a grammatical sentence.

A grammatical sentence need not make semantic sense. The deliberately nonsensical language examples separate satisfying grammar from understanding a plausible event. Similarly, a drawing can admit more than one coherent spatial interpretation. Constraints may leave several assignments or no assignment; they are not automatically a unique-answer mechanism.

citations.section: From Pixels to 3D; Line Labeling; Constraints Intersections and Edges

blocks.title: Line labeling turns junction knowledge into edge restrictions
blocks.text:
The visual task is decomposed into detecting lines, grouping them into oriented surfaces, and recognizing a three-dimensional object. The lesson concentrates on the middle step. A fold is an edge where two surfaces meet; a blade is an edge where that two-surface relationship is not inferred in the simplified scheme.

Prior knowledge specifies allowable label combinations for Y, W, L, and T junctions in the trihedral-object illustration. Its simplified Y junction has three folds; an L has two blades; a W has blade–fold–blade; the printed T rule has two blades and a fold. These are the teaching ontology’s selected patterns, not universal rules for every image. Assigning a shared edge’s label at one junction constrains which patterns are possible at the junction at its other end.

citations.section: Exercise Assembling the Cube I; Exercise Assembling the Cube II; More Complex Images

blocks.title: Propagate shared-edge consistency, then inspect conflicts
blocks.text:
Identify the cube drawing’s junction types, apply their permitted labels, and carry an edge’s label to adjacent junctions. A fold implies meeting surfaces; compatible labels across the drawing support grouping lines into the cube’s surfaces. The local junction rules thus contribute to a global interpretation.

A more complex image exposes the limited ontology: a line may be treated as a fold from one starting point and a blade from another, or may merely be a line drawn on a surface. The book explains that a richer set of junction constraints is needed. Richer constraints can also permit multiple consistent interpretations. A conflict is a reason to inspect the assumptions and representation, not arbitrarily erase the inconvenient label.

blocks.text:
Words are assigned lexical categories and grouped into phrases under grammar constraints. In the example, a noun phrase contains adjectives and a noun, while a verb phrase contains a verb and an optional adverb. Candidate phrase divisions must agree with lexical information and the grammar.

Top-down structural expectations and bottom-up word classifications support one another. A successful parse establishes grammatical compatibility, not that its nonsensical content is true or meaningful. Further semantic interpretation can use that structure. Across language and vision, constraint propagation is a general inference method whose results depend on the particular constraints supplied.

blocks.text: Constraint propagation connects local possibilities through shared variables and structural rules. The book’s visual and grammatical examples show both its power and why compatibility can be ambiguous or fail under an inadequate ontology.

chapters.title: Configuration
chapters.summary: Configuration is routine design with known components and constrained choices. Plan refinement assigns values at successive levels and evaluates the resulting arrangement.

citations.section: Define Design; Exercise Designing a Basement; Defining Configuration

blocks.title: Configuration is a design task, not one particular algorithm
blocks.text:
Design turns needs, goals, or functions into a specification of an artifact. In open-ended design, the problem and solution can evolve together. Configuration is the more routine case: the components or available component types are known, and the task is to assign their variables and arrange them under constraints.

The basement example distinguishes satisfying numerical area totals from producing a spatial layout that actually fits. A set of individually plausible room sizes is not necessarily a valid arrangement. Variable-order heuristics may begin with the most restricted, most influential, or most important choices, but those are control choices within the task rather than its definition.

citations.section: The Configuration Process; Example Representing a Chair; Example Ranges of Values

blocks.title: Refine a skeletal plan into a complete arrangement
blocks.text:
The illustrated method begins with a high-level design plan. Assign values to its variables, then refine and expand it into a more detailed plan with additional variables. Continue through an abstraction hierarchy until the arrangement is specified. Evaluation may return the process to earlier choices or expose an additional requirement.

A chair frame links to component frames for legs, seat, arms, and back. Variables include count, size or mass, material, and cost with allowed ranges. The source uses simplified gram-based sizes to make mass and material-cost calculations easy; these are teaching quantities, not realistic furniture specifications.

blocks.text:
A global cost or mass requirement must be distributed or checked across components. Another plan may choose material first instead of cost; there is no single mandatory variable order.

Constraints propagate through the plan hierarchy. A component change can affect the total cost or mass and require revision elsewhere. The final arrangement must be evaluated against the whole specification, not accepted because each slot has some value. Changing the specification is a design decision, not a silent way to count an invalid arrangement as a solution.

blocks.title: Plan refinement, classification, and case adaptation differ
blocks.text:
Refinement resembles establish-and-refine classification, but adds increasingly detailed component variables and their constraints. A planning process can generate a skeletal sequence or structure that configuration later instantiates.

Case-based design instead retrieves an existing arrangement and adapts it. Plan refinement starts from a plan abstraction hierarchy. Both can address routine design, and other reasoning methods may also be used. The task/method distinction explains why configuration should not be treated as a synonym for constraint propagation or for case-based reasoning.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Configuration combines known structure with constrained instantiation. A valid arrangement requires compatible component choices and satisfaction of global requirements, not merely a filled-in frame.

chapters.title: Diagnosis
chapters.summary: Diagnosis explains a discrepancy between expected and observed behavior. It maps data to fault hypotheses, compares competing explanations, and uses tests and repair feedback to refine them.

citations.section: Exercise Diagnosing Illness; Defining Diagnosis

blocks.title: Find the fault responsible for a malfunction
blocks.text:
Diagnosis begins when observed behavior differs from expected behavior. The task is to identify the fault or faults responsible. Rules, past cases, or a model of how the system works can support that task; diagnosis is not itself just one of those methods.

The lesson uses fictional disease names and abstract data letters to make competing explanations visible. Those examples are not health advice. Car and computer examples show the same task in other domains: explain the discrepancy, rather than merely attach a label to any observed symptom.

citations.section: Data Space and Hypothesis Space; Problems with Diagnosis as Classification

blocks.title: Data and hypotheses have a many-to-many relationship
blocks.text:
The data space contains observations and their abstractions. The hypothesis space contains candidate faults and their refinements. Bottom-up abstraction can organize observations, while top-down refinement can specialize a candidate explanation. The lesson calls their combination heuristic classification.

One observation may have several possible explanations, and one hypothesis may explain several observations. Hypotheses also predict further data worth collecting. Mutual exclusion means two hypotheses cannot both hold in the modeled situation; cancellation means combined effects can mask an expected observation. A diagnosis cannot therefore be chosen by matching one symptom to one label independently of the rest.

citations.section: Deduction, Induction, Abduction

blocks.title: Diagnosis is abductive, not the converse of a deduction
blocks.text:
Deduction uses a rule and its antecedent to derive a consequence. Induction generalizes a rule from observed relationships. Abduction uses an observed consequence and relevant knowledge to propose an explanation. A cause-to-effect implication does not license certainty about the cause when its effect is observed.

Different faults can produce the same behavior, so an abductive conclusion is a hypothesis rather than a truth-preserving deduction. An agent may combine abduction with deduction to predict additional observations and induction to revise relationships. Keeping these directions distinct prevents an explanatory guess from masquerading as a proof.

citations.section: Criteria for Choosing a Hypothesis; Exercise Diagnosis as Abduction

blocks.title: Balance coverage, parsimony, and confidence
blocks.text:
Explanatory coverage asks how much of the relevant data an explanation accounts for. Parsimony prefers a simpler explanation when other considerations are comparable. Confidence favors hypotheses supported more strongly or regarded as more likely. These can conflict: a single hypothesis may be simple but leave data unexplained, while a larger set covers more data at a cost.

The fictional examples combine hypotheses when needed and account for interactions that cancel effects. The goal is a coherent explanation of the whole observation set, not simply the fewest labels or the largest raw count of matching items. The source presents these as selection criteria, not a quantified probability formula.

citations.section: Completing the Process; Wrap Up

blocks.title: Testing and repair feed new evidence back into diagnosis
blocks.text:
A proposed fault can suggest additional observations or tests. Once a diagnosis is selected, it indexes a treatment or repair plan. Monitor the result: if replacing a suspected part does not restore the expected behavior, that failure becomes new diagnostic evidence.

Diagnosis therefore loops among data collection, hypotheses, and intervention rather than ending at the first plausible explanation. Repair and diagnosis remain different tasks. Restoring behavior can support an explanation, while failed intervention can reveal incomplete or mistaken assumptions.

chapters.title: Learning by Correcting Mistakes
chapters.summary: Learning by correcting mistakes isolates a suspicious knowledge feature, explains its role in failure, and repairs the model without damaging other valid knowledge.

citations.section: Exercise Identifying a Cup; Questions for Correcting Mistakes

blocks.title: A wrong answer starts learning; it does not finish it
blocks.text:
A robot classifies a pail as a cup and receives corrective feedback. It must identify the error, explain why that error led to the failure, and repair its knowledge. A mistaken rejection of a genuine cup poses the complementary problem. Both over-inclusion and under-inclusion can require revision.

Blame assignment identifies what in knowledge, reasoning, or architecture was responsible. This lesson concentrates on classification knowledge. A failed outcome alone does not reveal which of many distinguishing features caused it. Self-diagnosis makes this a step toward metacognition rather than merely diagnosis of another system.

citations.section: Visualizing Error Detection; Error Detection Algorithm

blocks.title: Contrast examples to find suspicious features
blocks.text:
A false success is something the agent accepted that should not have been accepted; a true success was correctly accepted. Features shared with correct cases are less useful for isolating why an accepted pail was wrong. Comparing more examples can eliminate incidental differences such as color.

The printed algorithm identifies suspicious false-success relations by intersecting features of the false successes and removing the union of true-success features. The complementary displayed calculation intersects true-success features and removes the union of false-success features. These operations identify contrasts in the supplied examples; they do not by themselves establish causality or guarantee that the representation contains the needed feature. The transcript mixes up these unions and intersections, so the printed algorithm is the locator for this summary.

blocks.title: A repaired classification must preserve the right explanation
blocks.text:
Adding “handle is fixed” to the cup rule can exclude the pail, but an unexplained extra condition does not say why it matters. The causal explanation locates the condition: a fixed handle supports manipulating and orienting the object for drinking, not liftability in general.

Placing the requirement under liftable would incorrectly deny that a pail or a briefcase with a movable handle can be lifted. The repair must therefore preserve valid background knowledge while changing the mistaken connection. The example shows why patching a decision rule and repairing its explanatory model are not equivalent.

Like incremental concept learning, corrective learning revises knowledge using examples. Here the agent’s own decision and the feedback it receives determine the learning need. Explanation connects the suspicious feature to the failure and guides a targeted repair.

The agent uses memory and reasoning to diagnose its model, then learns a change intended to improve future action. This is not a license to overfit one failure with arbitrary conditions. Additional examples and consistency with earlier explanations are essential when several candidate repairs remain.

chapters.title: Meta-Reasoning
chapters.summary: Meta-reasoning examines the agent’s own knowledge and processes, identifies errors or gaps, and selects or integrates methods to meet a task.

citations.section: Mistakes in Reasoning and Learning; Beyond Mistakes Knowledge Gaps; The Blurred Line Between Cognition and Metacognition

blocks.title: Errors and missing knowledge need different responses
blocks.text:
Meta-reasoning reasons about the agent’s own knowledge, reasoning, or learning. An incorrect connection needs repair; an absent connection needs acquisition. The mug explanation’s missing link from heat-transfer limitation to protection against heat is a knowledge gap, not evidence that every existing fragment is wrong.

Detecting that gap creates a learning goal: find knowledge that can connect the required conditions, whether from memory or an external source. A reasoning impasse can likewise create a goal to find a different method. Deliberation and metacognition can overlap; the crucial questions are what the process is acting on and what knowledge it uses, not forcing every operation into a disjoint box.

citations.section: Strategy Selection

blocks.title: Select a method using its requirements and consequences
blocks.text:
An agent may know several methods. Selection depends first on whether the required knowledge is available: cases for case-based reasoning, constraints for constraint propagation, or appropriate formal premises for logic. A method name does not make its missing knowledge appear.

Where multiple methods apply, computational efficiency and solution quality can matter. A close prior case may favor reuse; interacting goals can undermine a simple difference heuristic. The discussion also distinguishes incremental example arrival from batch data when choosing a learning method. Quality claims remain conditional on the method’s domain and assumptions, not an unconditional guarantee attached to a label.

citations.section: Strategy Integration; Process of Meta-Reasoning

blocks.title: Integrate methods across a task and its subtasks
blocks.text:
Selecting a method for the overall task does not prescribe every subtask’s method. Case-based reasoning can use rules, a model, or recursive retrieval for adaptation. A blocks-world obstacle can prompt problem reduction and then return to means-ends analysis on a selected subproblem.

Meta-reasoning can itself use familiar reasoning methods: recall how a similar strategy choice worked, plan a sequence of methods, or generate and evaluate alternative strategies. The distinction is the object of reasoning. Choosing a world action and choosing how to reason about that action can use similar mechanisms while operating on different content.

citations.section: Discussion Meta-Meta-Reasoning; Example Goal-Based Autonomy; Example Goal-Based Autonomy II

blocks.title: Flexible goals do not require an infinite tower of controllers
blocks.text:
The lesson rejects the need to posit a separate controller for every meta-level: a metacognitive process can reason about its own strategies recursively. That is an architectural proposal, not proof that monitoring has no computational cost.

Goal-based autonomy asks how an agent can respond to a new goal rather than fail brittly because it was programmed only for an older task. The camera-assembly example motivates reusing and adapting knowledge when asked to disassemble. Robustness comes from knowledge about strategies, their requirements, and the effects of changing them; it does not mean an agent can solve arbitrary tasks without new information.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Meta-reasoning makes an agent’s methods and knowledge objects of inquiry. It connects error repair, learning goals, method selection, and integration into a flexible but still knowledge-dependent architecture.

chapters.title: Advanced Topics
chapters.summary: Advanced topics connect perceptual representation, systems models, design, creativity, and ethics. They are extensions of the course’s methods, not claims that all open problems are solved.

citations.section: Visuospatial Reasoning Introduction; Two Views of Reasoning; Symbol Grounding Problem

blocks.title: Visuospatial content and its encoding are separate choices
blocks.text:
Visual knowledge concerns what is present; spatial knowledge concerns where it is and how it is arranged. Causality may be implicit: a spilled cup scene supports a causal inference without explicitly showing the spill process.

An agent can encode visuospatial content propositionally, using symbolic descriptions, or analogically, preserving structural correspondence with the perceptual situation. In this lesson analogical representation means a modal encoding, not analogical reasoning between source and target problems. The triangle example contrasts manipulating extracted symbolic descriptions with transformations of a structurally corresponding representation.

The symbol grounding problem concerns how symbols connect to what they stand for in perception and the world. Content being visual does not automatically make its encoding analogical, and naming an object does not explain how that name is grounded. The discussion introduces these issues rather than resolving all of them.

citations.section: Visuospatial Reasoning An Example; Visuospatial Reasoning Another Example; Ravens Progressive Matrices

blocks.title: Different models expose different information
blocks.text:
The Galatea example transfers a visuospatial procedure without first extracting the explicit causal pattern used in another account of the same thought experiment. Archytas instead uses known drawings and their models to transfer structure, behavior, and function to a new engineering drawing.

These are contrasting computational accounts of what is represented and transferred. The lesson also points to visual approaches to matrix problems. These historical systems illustrate research questions; the old project references and claims about the field describe the 2016 context, not current assignment scope or a survey of today’s systems.

citations.section: Systems Thinking Introduction; Systems Thinking Connections; Structure-Behavior-Function

blocks.title: Structure, behavior, and function explain a system
blocks.text:
A system contains interacting components whose processes may span several levels of abstraction. Observed structure alone may not reveal the invisible interactions that produce behavior. Systems thinking seeks an account of those relationships.

A Structure–Behavior–Function model separates components and connections, the causal processes or state transitions, and what the system achieves. The flashlight example identifies battery, switch, and bulb as structure; an enabled flow and energy conversion as behavior; and producing light as function. Models can be nested, with a component analyzed as a system at another level. This supports diagnosis and design because it explains how a structural change can affect an outcome.

citations.section: Design Introduction; Agents Doing Design

blocks.title: Open-ended design goes beyond configuring known parts
blocks.text:
Configuration arranges known components; more creative design may change the components or the understanding of the problem. Design thinking addresses ill-defined, underconstrained tasks with problem–solution coevolution.

The circuit discussion illustrates using a behavior model to propose a change, then learning and transferring a design pattern such as cascading components. Its simplified electrical and pump quantities illustrate pattern transfer, not a general engineering law or safe construction recipe. A candidate design still requires evaluation in its own domain.

citations.section: Creativity Introduction; Defining Creativity II; Exercise Defining Creativity III; Exercise Defining Creativity IV

blocks.title: Novelty, value, and unexpectedness are different criteria
blocks.text:
The creativity discussion distinguishes a new result, a useful or valuable result, and a non-obvious or surprising result. A larger batch of a familiar recipe may be new in one sense without being surprising. Creative products and the processes producing them are also different objects of study.

Analogy and explanation-based learning can support creative uses. Emergence reveals a property of a combined structure; re-representation changes how a problem is expressed to make new reasoning possible; serendipity connects an encountered opportunity to an earlier goal. These are examples, not an exhaustive list. Being generated by an explainable algorithm does not by itself disqualify an output as creative: context and the actual result matter.

citations.section: AI Ethics; Open Issues

blocks.title: Capability does not settle whether a system should be built
blocks.text:
The ethics discussion asks about effects on work and society, military uses and responsibility, and what criteria would matter when considering machines as human-like or as bearers of rights. These are questions for evaluating the consequences and values of AI development, not technical properties automatically established by a successful demonstration.

The chapter deliberately leaves open issues. A model of reasoning or creativity can clarify what a system does, but does not by itself resolve moral responsibility, distribution of benefits and harms, or justified deployment. Understanding these distinctions is part of the course, not an optional substitute for knowing the mechanisms.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: The advanced topics extend represent-and-reason to perceptual content, invisible system processes, and novel designs. They also distinguish explaining capability from evaluating its value and ethical consequences.

chapters.title: Wrap-Up
chapters.summary: The wrap-up reconnects the course through seven principles: organized knowledge, incremental learning, expectations, method-task fit, heuristics, recurring patterns, and unified reasoning–memory–learning.

citations.section: Cognitive Systems Revisited; Course Structure Revisited

blocks.title: Revisit the situated cognitive system
blocks.text:
Reaction, deliberation, and metacognition are overlapping spaces in an agent situated in a physical and social world. Reaction maps a percept to an action; deliberation mediates action through knowledge, memory, reasoning, and learning. Metacognition monitors and changes those internal processes.

A failed plan can lead to an alternative plan at the object level or to repairing the planner at the meta level. The course’s topics fit this larger architecture: representations make knowledge available, reasoning methods use it for tasks, learning changes it, and monitoring helps decide when methods or knowledge are inadequate.

citations.section: The First Principle; The Second Principle

blocks.title: Organized knowledge and incremental learning
blocks.text:
The first principle is represent, organize, and reason. Semantic networks expose relationships, frames organize expected roles, scripts organize event sequences, and composed explanations connect relevant knowledge fragments. Organization guides and focuses reasoning, not merely storage.

The second principle is that learning is often incremental. The printed figures revisit recorded cases, discrimination trees, concept revision, version spaces, and corrected explanations. Each new experience can change knowledge or its organization. Incremental does not mean every learning method uses identical updates or that no method needs batch data.

citations.section: The Third Principle; The Fourth Principle

blocks.title: Expectations and method-task fit guide processing
blocks.text:
The third principle combines bottom-up and top-down reasoning. Incoming cues activate knowledge structures, and those structures generate expectations about what to look for or infer. Frames, scripts, and constraints exemplify this interaction.

The fourth principle matches methods to tasks. A broad method such as generate and test is not automatically the best for every task; specialized knowledge may make another method more useful. Methods also create subtasks that can use different methods, so matching recurs throughout the task hierarchy. Meta-reasoning makes that selection and integration explicit.

citations.section: The Fifth Principle; The Sixth Principle

blocks.title: Heuristics and recurrence address resource limits
blocks.text:
The fifth principle uses heuristics for good-enough solutions under bounded resources. Satisficing seeks an adequate solution rather than exhaustive optimization when the latter is too expensive. The earlier limitations of means-ends analysis show why a heuristic’s usefulness is not a universal success guarantee.

The sixth principle exploits recurring patterns. Cases, analogies, and configuration plans reuse useful structure instead of solving every detail anew. Recurrence does not contradict novelty: an agent can transfer or adapt a known pattern to a new situation. The fit must still be evaluated.

citations.section: The Seventh Principle; Current Research

blocks.title: Reasoning, learning, and memory support and constrain one another
blocks.text:
The seventh principle unifies the three processes. Memory stores and organizes knowledge; learning acquires or changes it; reasoning uses it. The production-system impasse is the clearest example: reasoning cannot decide, memory supplies an episode, chunking learns a rule, and reasoning proceeds.

The corrected-cup and explanation examples show the same interdependence through different mechanisms. The listed research systems are historical pointers to further study, not a complete current inventory. The course closes with a framework for relating methods and identifying their knowledge requirements, not one algorithm that resolves every problem in intelligence.

weeks.title: Introduction to Knowledge-Based AI & Introduction to CS7637
weeks.notes:
Knowledge-based AI asks how limited agents use knowledge to understand situations and choose actions. The introduction connects reasoning, learning, and memory; the course overview then uses visual analogy to expose different ways an agent might solve the same problem. Read these together as the course’s organizing framework, not a list of unrelated AI techniques.

The starting point is a task, represented knowledge, and a reasoning process. Human-like cognition and rational task performance are distinct aims. The seven course principles connect what follows: organize knowledge, learn incrementally, use expectations, match methods to tasks, work within resource limits, exploit recurring patterns, and connect reasoning with memory and learning.

weeks.title: Semantic Networks & Generate & Test
weeks.notes:
Semantic networks describe the objects, relationships, and states an agent reasons about. Generate and test explains how it uses that description to propose and reject possibilities. Together they introduce represent-and-reason: a useful notation makes the task computable, but a method must still decide what to do with it.

A network can describe spatial relations, transformations, or a state space. A generator proposes candidates and a tester evaluates them. The source’s recurring-state and ambiguity examples show why legal states, productive search, and preferred matches are different judgments.

weeks.title: Means-Ends Analysis & Production Systems
weeks.notes:
This week asks how an agent decides what to do next. Means-ends analysis uses the difference between a current state and a goal to guide search; problem reduction tackles a complex goal through smaller problems. Production systems then give a concrete architecture in which current facts and goals activate rules. The connection is action selection: the blocks world exposes unresolved choices, and the pitcher example shows how an architecture can use memory and learning when its rules cannot decide.

Across these lessons, a goal is not enough to determine an action. The agent also needs a representation, available operators or rules, and knowledge for choosing between alternatives. The limits of a difference heuristic motivate subproblems and, later, planning; the limits of an existing rule set motivate an impasse and chunking. Keep the two levels separate: searching a world-state space is not the same as changing the knowledge used to search or act.

weeks.title: Frames & Learning by Recording Cases
weeks.notes:
Frames organize expectations about a situation into slots and fillers. Recording cases organizes past experiences so a similar problem can retrieve a candidate answer. Both lessons show how memory supplies useful structure, but neither defaults nor a nearest case should be confused with a guaranteed fact or unchanged solution.

Frames supply a structured expectation to be filled and corrected; cases supply a remembered experience selected through a similarity representation. Defaults remain defeasible, and distance measures remain task-dependent. A retrieved route can still need adaptation even if it is the nearest one.

weeks.title: Case-Based Reasoning
weeks.notes:
Case-based reasoning turns remembered experience into a complete problem-solving process. The key addition to last week’s retrieval is reasoning about differences: adapt an old solution, evaluate the candidate, and decide what useful experience to store. The route examples keep these roles separate and show where failure sends the process back.

Reuse is not copying. Adaptation uses a world model, other cases, or rules; evaluation checks the current requirements. Indices and discrimination trees make cases retrievable, while selective storage avoids treating every added case as an improvement.

weeks.title: Incremental Concept Learning & Classification
weeks.notes:
Incremental concept learning explains how a concept changes as labeled examples arrive. Classification explains how organized concepts are then used to interpret percepts and guide action. The connection is abstraction: a learner moves beyond individual cases, but the kind of concept determines what a definition and a classification method can legitimately do.

Generalization repairs a missed positive; specialization repairs a covered negative. Background knowledge and heuristics guide that revision. Classification then uses formal conditions, defeasible prototypes, or exemplars as appropriate, with top-down refinement or bottom-up abstraction fitted to the task.

weeks.title: Logic
weeks.notes:
Logic makes the knowledge and inference steps of an agent explicit. Start with statements and connectives, use truth tables to justify equivalent rewrites, then follow the robot’s resolution proof. This week also includes Exam 1 review of Lessons 01–12.

A knowledge base states premises; an inference engine derives what follows. Quantifiers express scope, while the worked resolution examples return to propositional clauses and refute a negated conclusion. For the earlier lessons, keep representations, reasoning methods, architectures, and learning processes distinct: a network is not a generator, a frame default is not a theorem, and retrieval is not adaptation.

weeks.title: Planning & Understanding
weeks.notes:
Planning and understanding both use structured knowledge to resolve choices. Planning coordinates actions whose effects and preconditions can interfere; understanding coordinates grammatical cues and thematic roles to select an interpretation. Both build on earlier representations while making the source of each constraint explicit.

Planning resolves the goal interactions left open in means-ends analysis and problem reduction. Understanding resolves meaning through role constraints and background knowledge. A compatible plan must support its required conditions; a compatible interpretation must fit the actual sentence and context.

weeks.title: Commonsense Reasoning & Scripts
weeks.notes:
Commonsense reasoning abstracts surface wording into primitive actions and resultant states. Scripts connect those event frames into familiar sequences, such as a restaurant visit. Together the lessons move from understanding one action to understanding a longer story and predicting what should happen next.

Different words can share an underlying action without having identical connotations. Primitive frames capture roles and effects; scripts add entry conditions, results, props, roles, tracks, and scenes. Expected events can fail to happen, and unexpected events can happen: both require comparing stored expectations with the actual situation.

weeks.title: Explanation-Based Learning & Analogical Reasoning
weeks.notes:
Explanation-based learning and analogical reasoning use prior knowledge to address something new. The first composes causal fragments to explain why an object fits a required concept. The second retrieves a source, maps corresponding relations, and transfers useful knowledge across domains. Both need a justified connection, not merely a resemblance.

Abstraction selects what matters from a source; transfer applies it where the target’s conditions support it. The mug’s missing link stays a gap, and a cross-domain analogy remains a proposal until evaluated. Compound and compositional analogies show that transfer can involve several sources or several levels rather than one copied answer.

weeks.title: Version Spaces & Constraint Propagation
weeks.notes:
Version spaces constrain alternative concept hypotheses using labeled examples. Constraint propagation constrains alternative interpretations using shared variables and structural rules. The common idea is to make possibilities explicit and eliminate incompatible ones, while keeping the two kinds of evidence distinct.

Examples restrict what a learned concept can cover; junction and grammatical constraints restrict which assignments can coexist. Version-space convergence needs informative consistent evidence and an adequate hypothesis form. Propagation can leave multiple interpretations or reveal conflicts under an inadequate ontology. Neither method should be presented as a guarantee of one true answer in every problem.

weeks.title: Configuration & Diagnosis
weeks.notes:
Configuration and diagnosis are tasks that can use several reasoning methods. Configuration seeks an arrangement of known components satisfying requirements; diagnosis seeks fault explanations for a discrepancy in behavior. The chair and malfunction examples connect representations, global constraints, evaluation, and feedback.

Configuration refines a candidate arrangement and checks the whole specification. Diagnosis compares explanatory coverage, parsimony, and confidence and can request further observations. Designing a change and explaining a failure are different tasks, even when both use cases, rules, constraints, or models.

weeks.title: Learning by Correcting Mistakes & Meta-Reasoning
weeks.notes:
Learning by correcting mistakes uses feedback to identify and repair an agent’s own mistaken knowledge. Meta-reasoning broadens that idea to errors, gaps, method selection, and strategy integration. The connection is self-directed inquiry: a failed result identifies a problem to investigate, not a magic instruction that repairs the agent automatically.

A suspicious feature is not yet a causal explanation. The corrected-cup example shows why repair must preserve valid distinctions such as liftable versus suitable for drinking. Meta-reasoning then turns missing knowledge into learning goals and chooses methods according to their requirements, costs, and supported solution quality.

weeks.title: Advanced Topics
weeks.notes:
Advanced Topics connects visuospatial representation, systems thinking, design, creativity, and ethics. These are not five replacement algorithms: they extend the course’s questions about what is represented, how an explanation is built, how novel solutions are evaluated, and what consequences of capability deserve scrutiny.

Keep content separate from encoding, analogical representation separate from analogical reasoning, and structure separate from behavior and function. Design can change the problem as well as the solution; creativity involves distinct judgments of novelty, value, and unexpectedness. Technical success does not resolve ethical questions about using an agent.

weeks.title: Consolidation & final project
weeks.notes:
There are no new lessons this week. Consolidate the course’s representations, reasoning methods, and evaluation ideas alongside the final ARC-AGI project. The earlier weekly notes remain available by topic.

Connect the representation an agent uses with the reasoning it affords, the experiences it can retrieve, and the evidence used to evaluate a result. Configuration, diagnosis, analogy, and meta-reasoning offer different perspectives on that connection.

weeks.title: Revision & Exam 2
weeks.notes:
There are no new lessons this week. Review Lessons 13–25 for Exam 2, including earlier concepts where they support those later mechanisms. Focus on how each method uses knowledge and what its conclusions do and do not establish.

Planning coordinates conditions and effects; understanding and scripts coordinate meaning and expectations; explanation and analogy justify transfer; version spaces and constraints retain compatible possibilities; configuration and diagnosis address different tasks; corrective learning and meta-reasoning revise the agent’s own knowledge and methods.

weeks.title: Wrap-Up
weeks.notes:
Wrap-Up reconnects the whole course through the cognitive-system architecture and seven recurring principles. This week adds synthesis, not another isolated method: organized knowledge, incremental learning, top-down expectations, method-task fit, heuristics, recurring patterns, and the unity of reasoning, memory, and learning explain how the earlier topics fit together.

The useful final picture is an agent situated in a changing world, selecting actions through representations and methods it can learn, retrieve, and monitor. Understanding KBAI means being able to explain those relationships and their limits, rather than recognizing twenty-six disconnected lesson titles.
